title: China's Data Dominance Gives It AI Edge Over U.S., Congressional Report Warns
excerpt: A U.S.-China commission says Beijing is treating data as a national strategic asset, collecting real-world information that American companies cannot scrape from the open internet.
body:
• The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission warns that China is treating data as a strategic national asset, giving it a potential edge in the AI race.
  • While U.S. companies have largely exhausted open internet data for training, China is systematically collecting enterprise, operational, and physical-world data that cannot be scraped.
  • China's manufacturing and robotics ecosystems generate high-quality data for embodied AI — systems that operate in the physical world, such as autonomous vehicles and humanoid robots.
  • The commission's top recommendation is for Congress to develop a national data strategy treating data as an economic asset.

A U.S. congressional advisory body warned on Tuesday that China is systematically commercializing and monetizing data as a strategic national asset, a push that could hand Beijing a decisive advantage in the global AI race — particularly in robotics, autonomous vehicles, and industrial applications.

The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission's report, released on August 18, found that Beijing is "marshalling data to drive productivity" while simultaneously improving "its intelligence collection and military capabilities."

A Data Gap the U.S. Cannot Scrape Away

The report identifies a fundamental asymmetry. Major U.S. AI companies have largely exhausted the open internet for language model training. China, by contrast, is collecting domestic "enterprise, operational and physical-world data that cannot be scraped" — the kind of proprietary, real-world information crucial for training AI tools designed for business use, factory automation, and autonomous systems.

"Over the last half decade, China has been able to consolidate data, find ways to label it and refine it, and hoover up new data and make sure it's quickly made available to entities."

— Mike Kuiken, Vice Chair, U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission

China's advanced manufacturing and industrial robotics ecosystems provide a vast pool of high-quality data for use in embodied AI applications — AI systems that operate in the physical world, such as robots — giving it a potential advantage over the U.S. in developing robotics software for both commercial and military uses, according to Reuters.

Data as a Factor of Production

China has elevated data to a core "factor of production" alongside land, labor, capital, and technology. In 2023, Beijing established the National Data Administration to oversee nationwide data standardization and classification and to build a unified national market for data trading.

Chinese firms have begun listing their proprietary datasets on regional data exchanges in cities including Shanghai, Shenzhen, and Beijing. The government aims to standardize data assets across critical industries — manufacturing, transport, finance, and healthcare — creating a structured national data infrastructure with no clear U.S. equivalent.

"It has the benefit of advancing their innovation ecosystem, and it has the benefit of enhancing the control of the (Chinese Communist) Party," Kuiken said in an interview with Reuters.

From Open-Source Dominance to Embodied AI

The new report builds on an earlier March 2026 finding by the same commission that China's open-source AI dominance was creating a "self-reinforcing competitive advantage." Chinese large language models from firms including Alibaba, Moonshot, and MiniMax now dominate worldwide usage rankings on platforms like HuggingFace and OpenRouter. An estimated 80% of U.S. AI startups use Chinese open-source models.

DeepSeek's R1 model overtook ChatGPT as the most downloaded model on the U.S. App Store last year, while Alibaba's Qwen family has surpassed Meta's Llama in global cumulative downloads, according to HuggingFace data.

As AI's frontier shifts from language models toward agentic AI and embodied AI, China's mass data collection efforts could prove particularly valuable. The commission noted that Beijing's push to deploy AI across manufacturing, logistics, and robotics is generating real-world data that feeds back into model improvement — a virtuous cycle the U.S. has been slower to replicate.

The Policy Prescription

"We recommend that U.S. Congress think about a national data strategy and how the U.S. government could treat data as an economic asset as our number one recommendation," Kuiken said.

The report also flagged risks for U.S. firms operating in China, noting that Beijing's strict cross-border data regulations have forced companies to localize their China subsidiaries and separate Chinese customer data from global operations. While limited exemptions exist, U.S. firms "risk running afoul of China's strict data and cyber governance regimes."

The findings arrive amid escalating U.S.-China technology tensions. Washington has imposed successive rounds of export restrictions on advanced AI chips since 2022, and the State Department is preparing to press dozens of countries to choose sides in the AI race, warning that membership in China's rival framework is incompatible with the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative.
